title: CAN YOU TRULY REPENT WHILE ALREADY PLANNING TO COMMIT THE SAME SIN AGAIN?
paragraphs: CAN YOU TRULY REPENT WHILE ALREADY PLANNING TO COMMIT THE SAME SIN AGAIN?
The Terrifying Difference Between Falling Into Sin and Secretly Making Room for It—And Why Jesus Still Offers Grace to the Person Who Is Tired of Living a Double Life.
There is a kind of prayer that sounds like repentance but hides a terrible secret.
“Lord, please forgive me.”

The words are sincere enough to bring tears. Your chest feels heavy. Your conscience is screaming. You know what you did was wrong. You know it wounded your relationship with God. You know you crossed a line you promised yourself you would never cross again.
But somewhere beneath those tears, another conversation is already happening.
Maybe just one more time.
Maybe after this weekend.
Maybe I'll stop when things settle down.
Maybe God will understand.
And suddenly, the most frightening question is not whether God can forgive your sin.
It is whether you have actually decided to leave it.
Because what happens when your mouth is asking Jesus for forgiveness while your heart is quietly reserving a place for the very thing that nailed Him to the cross?
What happens when you kneel before God in the morning but have already made arrangements to disobey Him that night?
And what if the reason you keep returning to the same sin is not simply that you are weak—but that a part of you still loves what you keep asking God to remove?
Read that again.
Not because I want to condemn you.
But because somewhere, someone is exhausted from living two lives.
The life everyone sees.
And the life only God knows.
Perhaps that someone is you.
You love Jesus. At least, you believe you do. You listen to worship music. You share Bible verses. You know how to pray. You know what is right.
But there is a particular sin that keeps finding its way back into your life.

Maybe it is pornography. A secret relationship. Dishonesty. Sexual immorality. Gambling. Bitterness. A hidden addiction. An unforgiving heart. A habit of manipulating people. A pattern of gossip. A relationship you know is leading you away from obedience.
Perhaps nobody suspects anything.
You still smile in church.
You still say, “God is good.”
You still encourage other people to trust Him.
But when the room becomes quiet and the phone is in your hand, when temptation whispers your name, when the opportunity presents itself again, something inside you begins negotiating.
And you know exactly where that negotiation usually ends.
Afterward comes the familiar silence.
The shame.
The promise.
The prayer.
“Jesus, I'm sorry. I won't do it again.”
Until the next time.
But here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Struggling with a sin you desperately want to overcome is not the same as deliberately planning a sin you have no intention of surrendering.
Those two conditions may look similar from the outside.
But spiritually, they are not the same.
And confusing them can destroy a person's understanding of repentance, grace, and the Gospel itself.
The Bible does not teach that a genuinely repentant Christian will never stumble again. If that were true, the apostle John would never have written:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, KJV
And he continues:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say that Christians never sin.
He does not say that forgiveness is available only to those who have achieved perfect obedience.
He points us toward confession, God's faithfulness, and the cleansing made possible through Jesus Christ.
Yet this same apostle also writes:
Do you see the beauty and seriousness of those words?
That ye sin not.
And then:
If any man sin.
God's grace is not permission to pursue sin.
It is hope for the sinner who needs a Savior.
Jesus is our Advocate, not our accomplice.
He does not stand beside us to bless our rebellion. He stands for those who come to Him because His righteousness and atoning sacrifice are their only hope.
And this brings us to the word that changes everything.
Repentance.
In the Greek New Testament, the noun commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), and the related verb is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
The language speaks of a change of mind or understanding that, in biblical calls to repentance, involves a fundamental turning toward God.
Not merely feeling bad.
Not simply being embarrassed because someone discovered your secret.
Not crying because your actions produced painful consequences.
Biblical repentance involves a changed response to God, sin, and the truth.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
In the Greek text, the command includes:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Two commands that belong together.
Turn from your rebellion toward God.
Believe the good news of what Jesus Christ has accomplished.
Repentance is not an attempt to purchase salvation through better behavior. Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ, not earned by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the grace that saves us does not leave sin unchallenged.
Ephesians 2:10 reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up so Jesus will finally love you.”
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners—and calls those who trust Him into a new life.
This is where the difference between regret and repentance becomes painfully personal.
Regret says, “I hate what happened to me because of my sin.”
Repentance says, “Lord, I have sinned against You, and I want to turn from it.”
Regret may mourn the consequences.
Repentance recognizes the offense against God.
Regret may wish the evidence would disappear.
Repentance becomes willing to bring what is hidden into the light.
And sometimes both feelings exist in the same broken heart.
That is why we must never pretend to know every person's spiritual condition from a single failure.
God sees what human eyes cannot.
But Scripture gives us a serious warning about sorrow that never becomes surrender.
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” — 2 Corinthians 7:10, KJV
The Greek expression translated “godly sorrow” is ἡ κατὰ θεὸν λύπη (hē kata theon lypē)—sorrow according to God.
Paul's point is not that tears automatically prove repentance.
He describes sorrow that produces repentance.
A grief that leads somewhere.
A sorrow that stops making excuses.
A conviction that begins changing the direction of a life.
And that distinction matters because you can be genuinely emotional without being genuinely willing to change.
You can cry because you lost a relationship while still refusing to abandon the behavior that destroyed it.
You can feel ashamed after watching pornography while already deciding when you will return to it.
You can apologize for lying while secretly preparing your next deception.
You can ask God to forgive an affair while continuing to arrange private meetings with the person involved.
And you can feel miserable about all of it.
But misery alone is not repentance.
Now comes the question many people are afraid to ask.
If I already know I am going to commit the same sin again, can my repentance still be genuine?
The answer depends on what you mean by know.
If you mean, “I am afraid I might fall again because I know how weak I am,” that fear does not automatically make your repentance false.
A believer may sincerely turn from sin and still struggle with temptation, ingrained habits, addiction, or patterns that require sustained spiritual and practical help.
But if you mean, “I have already decided to do it again, and I am asking forgiveness now because I expect God to excuse my future disobedience,” that is something entirely different.
That is not simply weakness.
It is a deliberate intention to continue in what you acknowledge as sin.
And that intention contradicts the turning of heart that repentance requires.
You cannot sincerely say, “Lord, I am turning away from this,” while deliberately planning to keep walking toward it.
You may be beginning to feel conviction.
You may be experiencing the first painful signs of spiritual awakening.
You may even be wrestling with the desire to surrender.
But you should not call a settled plan to continue sinning the same thing as repentance.
This does not mean God's mercy has become unreachable.
It means you need to stop disguising your refusal as surrender.
And the astonishing thing is that you can bring even that divided heart to Jesus.
You can pray:

“Lord, I know this is wrong. Part of me still wants it. I have made excuses. I am afraid of losing what this sin gives me. I cannot honestly tell You that all my desires are pure. But I do not want to keep hiding. Expose what I have been protecting. Teach me to hate what is destroying me. Help me turn to You.”
That is not a polished religious performance.
That is spiritual honesty.
And honesty is a far better beginning than another promise you are not prepared to keep.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that helps us understand this turning.
שׁוּב (shuv).
It commonly means “to turn” or “to return.”
In the Old Testament, it is frequently used when God calls His people to turn away from evil and return to Him.
Through the prophet Isaiah, the Lord declares:

“Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.” — Isaiah 55:7, KJV
Look at the movement of the verse.
Forsake.
Return.
Mercy.
Pardon.
The command is not merely to feel differently about the road.
It is to leave the road and return to the Lord.
And notice that God calls the wicked to return because mercy is available.
Not because the wicked have somehow made themselves worthy.
Not because they have accumulated enough good deeds.
But because the Lord is merciful.
This is the heartbeat of biblical repentance.
Turning from sin and returning to God.
Yet some people hear this and immediately begin drowning in fear.
“What if I repented yesterday and sinned again today?”
“What if I have confessed the same thing a hundred times?”
“What if I am fighting an addiction and keep relapsing?”
“What if I genuinely want to change, but I still experience sinful desires?”
Listen carefully.
The presence of temptation does not prove the absence of repentance.
And a repeated failure does not, by itself, prove that every previous confession was a lie.
The Bible does not teach that repentance means temptation instantly disappears.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
Temptation and sin are not identical.
Nor does Scripture teach that the Christian life is sustained by human willpower alone.
Galatians 5:16 calls believers to walk in the Spirit.
Romans 8:13 teaches that by the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the body.
The battle is real.
The responsibility is real.
And the help of God is real.
There is a difference between a person who falls while resisting temptation and a person who deliberately builds a comfortable home for sin.
One may cry, “Lord, help me stand.”
The other may quietly whisper, “Lord, forgive me, but do not interfere with my plans.”
And sometimes the most frightening reality is that we can move from one condition toward the other without noticing.
The first time, we tremble.
The second time, we rationalize.
The third time, we prepare.
Eventually, what once troubled our conscience begins to feel ordinary.
That is why Hebrews 3:13 warns about being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying, “I am here to destroy your relationship with God.”
It says, “You deserve this.”
“It is not that serious.”
“Everybody struggles.”
“You can repent later.”
“God understands.”
And the most dangerous lie of all:
“Because God is gracious, you do not need to change.”
But Paul confronts that exact distortion.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The Greek response translated “God forbid” is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It is an emphatic rejection, expressing something like, “Absolutely not!”
Paul refuses the idea that grace should become an excuse for continuing in sin.
Why?
Because believers have been united with Christ in His death and resurrection.
Grace does not simply change the consequences of sin.
It establishes a new relationship to sin through Jesus Christ.
The Christian may still struggle.
But sin is no longer to be embraced as master.
And perhaps this is where the article has become uncomfortable.
Because you are remembering something.
A conversation you should not have continued.
A website you keep revisiting.
A message you deleted.
A financial decision you have been concealing.
A person you keep contacting even though you know the relationship is pulling you toward disobedience.
A private habit you have learned to justify with public spirituality.
You have prayed about it.
You have cried about it.
You have promised to stop.
But have you actually begun removing the things that keep leading you back?
Jesus said:
“And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee.” — Matthew 5:29, KJV
Jesus uses deliberately shocking imagery to communicate the seriousness of dealing with sin. This is not a command to physically injure yourself.
It is a call to take radical, decisive action against what leads you into sin.
Sometimes that means deleting an app.
Sometimes it means ending a secret relationship.
Sometimes it means surrendering access to something you repeatedly misuse.
Sometimes it means confessing the truth to a trustworthy, mature Christian who can help you walk in accountability.
Sometimes it means seeking qualified counseling or addiction treatment alongside prayer and pastoral support.
Sometimes it means making restitution for what you have stolen or correcting a lie that harmed someone.
Not because those actions earn forgiveness.
But because repentance is not merely something we claim with our lips.
It bears fruit in the way we respond to sin.
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.” — Matthew 3:8, KJV
The Greek expression includes καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας (karpon axion tēs metanoias)—fruit worthy of repentance.
Fruit is not the root of salvation.
But genuine repentance is not indifferent to fruit.
And if you are unwilling to change anything that makes your sin easier, you should seriously examine whether you have surrendered that sin at all.
Now I want to take you somewhere.
Not to a theological classroom.
Not to a church platform.
But to a courtyard.
A cold night.
A fire burning.
A frightened disciple trying to survive.
His name was Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had seen miracles.
He had heard the voice of the Son of God.
He had confidently declared that he would remain faithful.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied even knowing Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And Luke records one of the most devastating moments in the Gospels.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that look.
Peter had just denied the One he loved.
And Jesus turned toward him.
We are not told every expression that crossed the Savior's face. Scripture does not give us permission to invent His thoughts.
But it tells us what happened next.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62, KJV
Peter broke.
The confident disciple who had insisted he would never fall now had to face what he had done.
But here is something essential.
Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus questioned him about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter did not restore himself by pretending the denial never happened.
And Jesus did not treat Peter's failure as proof that restoration was impossible.
The risen Christ graciously restored a fallen disciple.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The same Jesus who knows your worst failure is the Savior who calls sinners to Himself.
But do not confuse Peter's restoration with permission to plan your own denial.
Peter's story is not an invitation to betray Jesus because you expect forgiveness afterward.
It is a testimony that even grievous failure need not have the final word when Christ restores a repentant sinner.
And then there is Judas.
Another disciple.
Another betrayal.
Another man who experienced devastating remorse.
Matthew 27:3 tells us that Judas regretted what he had done and returned the thirty pieces of silver.
He acknowledged that he had betrayed innocent blood.
Yet the biblical account does not portray Judas turning in saving faith to the risen Christ.
His story ends in tragedy.
We should not reduce the contrast between Peter and Judas to a simplistic claim that one cried the right kind of tears while the other cried the wrong kind.
The accounts are more profound than that.
Peter's story includes Christ's gracious restoration.
Judas's story demonstrates the terrible seriousness of betrayal and remorse without the restoration we see in Peter.
The lesson is not that you must manufacture a certain emotional intensity to be forgiven.
It is that remorse alone is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And you must come to Him.
Not simply to your guilt.
Not merely to your shame.
Not to a performance of religious sorrow.
To Christ Himself.
Because the cross is not a place where sin is treated lightly.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the mercy of God meet in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
He was not crucified because sin was harmless.
He gave Himself for sinners because sin is deadly, and we could not rescue ourselves.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every broken thing.
Not after we had earned the right to approach Him.
While we were sinners.
And because Christ died and rose again, forgiveness is not an empty religious wish.
It is grounded in the finished work of the Savior.
Still, someone reading this may be asking:
“But what if I keep falling?”
Then do not make peace with falling.
Keep bringing your sin into the light.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep praying.
Keep seeking the help you need.
Keep taking concrete steps to remove temptation.
And when you fall, do not use the fall as an excuse to abandon the fight.
Confess your sin.
Turn again to Christ.
Remember that your hope is not in the perfection of your repentance but in the sufficiency of your Savior.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It keeps repentance from becoming another attempt to save yourself.
Jesus does not tell us to trust in the emotional strength of our sorrow.
He tells us to believe the Gospel.
And perhaps the most hopeful picture of repentance appears in the story of the prodigal son.
He had demanded his inheritance.
Left his father's house.
Wasted his wealth.
And eventually found himself hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
Then Luke 15:17 says:
“And when he came to himself...”
What a sentence.
He came to himself.
He stopped pretending.
He saw where his choices had taken him.
He recognized what he had lost.
And he decided to return.
But notice what happened next.
He did not merely sit among the pigs feeling guilty.
He got up.
He went home.
And while he was still a great way off, his father saw him, had compassion, ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.
That is the picture Jesus gave.
Not of a father who approved of rebellion.
Not of a father who pretended the son had done nothing wrong.
But of a father whose mercy welcomed a returning son.
And perhaps today you have been sitting in the same spiritual pigpen, rehearsing apologies while refusing to stand up.
You keep saying you miss the Father's house.
But you keep making plans to stay in the far country.
The invitation is not to become worthy before returning.
It is to get up and come home.
And if your heart is divided, tell Him.
If you are afraid to surrender, tell Him.
If you still feel attracted to the sin, tell Him.
If you have spent years performing Christianity while hiding a secret life, stop pretending that God is surprised.
He already knows.
And still, through the Gospel, the call to repent and believe goes out.
This is what makes grace so astonishing.
God's mercy is not reserved for people with impressive spiritual histories.
Christ came to save sinners.
But His grace must never be turned into an excuse to remain deliberately enslaved to the very sins from which He calls us.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
Grace is not merely pardon.
It also trains us.
It reshapes us.
It teaches us to say no to what once ruled us.
Not instantly in every struggle.
Not without painful battles.
But genuinely.
And here is a question worth sitting with tonight.
If Jesus removed every consequence you feared from your favorite sin, would you still want to stop doing it because you love Him?
Do not rush past that.
Would you still want to obey if nobody could discover your secret?
Would you still want purity if there were no embarrassment?
Would you still want honesty if the lie could never be exposed?
Would you still want holiness if disobedience brought you temporary pleasure without immediate earthly consequences?
That question may reveal something about what you love.
But if your answer frightens you, do not despair.
Bring that answer to God.
Ask Him to change not only your behavior but your desires.
David prayed after his grievous sin:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
In Hebrew:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים וְרוּחַ נָכוֹן חַדֵּשׁ בְּקִרְבִּי
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim, veruach nakhon chaddesh beqirbi.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
David did not merely ask for his reputation to be restored.
He asked for a clean heart.
A renewed spirit.
Something deeper than damage control.
And perhaps that is what you need to ask for today.
Not simply, “Lord, make the consequences disappear.”
But, “Lord, change the heart that keeps choosing this.”
Not simply, “Lord, forgive me so I can feel better.”
But, “Lord, teach me to love You more than I love this sin.”
Not simply, “Lord, let me escape being exposed.”
But, “Lord, lead me into the truth, even when truth requires painful obedience.”
That is a prayer worth praying.
And it may be the beginning of a very different story.
A story in which the person who once concealed an addiction finally asks for help.
The husband who lived dishonestly begins telling the truth.
The woman who kept returning to a destructive relationship finally establishes boundaries.
The believer who has been consumed by bitterness begins the difficult journey toward forgiveness.
The person who has been using grace as an excuse finally recognizes that grace is calling them into freedom.
Not every story resolves overnight.
Some battles require years of faithful perseverance, wise support, and ongoing dependence on the Holy Spirit.
Some broken relationships cannot be repaired simply because we apologize.
Some consequences remain even after God forgives.
And repentance does not guarantee that other people must immediately trust us again.
But none of that makes transformation meaningless.
Jesus is not offering a cosmetic improvement to a religious image.
He calls us to a new life in Him.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That new identity is grounded in being united to Christ.
It does not mean every temptation instantly vanishes.
It means that your past sin does not have the authority to define who you are in Him.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
And that is why we keep proclaiming the message at the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He erases the need for repentance.
Not because His forgiveness makes deliberate rebellion harmless.
But because His death and resurrection provide the only foundation for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and genuine transformation.
He rewrites lives by redeeming sinners, not by renaming sin as righteousness.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not need to tell strangers the details of your private struggles.
You do not need to expose another person's sin.
But perhaps you need to stop pretending that everything is fine.
And if you have experienced the mercy of Jesus after a season of wandering, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to make your spiritual life a performance.
But because someone else may be sitting alone tonight, believing they are beyond the reach of grace.
Your testimony might remind them to turn to Christ.
And if you know someone who is struggling with the difference between conviction and condemnation, send them this article privately.
If someone came to mind while reading, consider tagging them only if doing so would encourage them without exposing or embarrassing them.
One conversation may encourage someone to seek help.
One biblical reminder may interrupt a dangerous decision.
One testimony may point a wandering heart back toward Jesus.
Not as a substitute for opening your Bible.
But as a reminder to return to the Word, resist sin, and remember the mercy of Christ.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Because the Gospel is not merely for people who already look religious.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
There is also another way to help this ministry continue reaching people.

Scripture teaches that supporting faithful ministry is a worthy use of our resources. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or compelled.
That balance matters.
It does not purchase His favor.
And it should not replace your responsibilities to your local church, family, or those in need.
What we can say is this:
That is a meaningful opportunity to glorify God through generosity—not because God needs your money, but because we can use what He has entrusted to us in service to others.
These resources can become everyday reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share encouragement with others.
That free access matters.
Because the purpose is not to put spiritual growth behind a payment.
It is to make biblical resources available while inviting those who are able to help sustain and expand the work.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite others to read Scripture.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Every sincere act of service has value, even when no money changes hands.
But before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought us here.
Can you truly repent while already planning to commit the same sin again?
If you are deliberately holding on to a plan to sin, refusing to abandon it, and treating future forgiveness as permission, you are contradicting the very turning that repentance requires.
Do not call that surrender.
But if you are sincerely turning toward Christ, even while trembling at the possibility of another failure, do not mistake your weakness for proof that His mercy is unavailable.
Run to Jesus.
Not away from Him.
Do not plan your next sin and presume upon grace.
And do not let your last failure persuade you to abandon the Savior.
Confess what is true.
Forsake what you can no longer honestly defend.
Seek the help you need.
Trust in Christ and His finished work.
Walk in the Spirit.
And when the battle becomes difficult, remember that the One who calls you to repentance is also the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
Perhaps tonight you need to pray a prayer you have avoided for years.

“Father, I have called it weakness when sometimes it was deliberate disobedience. I have asked for forgiveness while protecting the things that lead me back into sin. Forgive me for treating Your mercy casually. I cannot cleanse my own heart. I need Jesus Christ, my Savior. Give me a hatred for what dishonors You and a greater love for what pleases You. Help me stop hiding, stop negotiating, and start obeying. Give me courage to seek help, make things right where possible, and walk in the truth. When I am weak, teach me to depend on Your Spirit. And when I fall, lead me to honest confession rather than despair. Thank You for the cross, for the resurrection, and for the hope of forgiveness through Jesus Christ. Amen.”
And now, one final thought.
There may come a moment tonight when temptation returns.
The screen will light up.
The message will arrive.
The old desire will awaken.
The familiar excuse will begin forming in your mind.
And you will stand at a crossroads that nobody else can see.
You may not feel powerful.
You may not feel holy.
You may not feel anything at all.
But by God's grace, you can choose to turn toward Christ instead of preparing another excuse.
And if you need help, reach for it before you fall, not only after.
Because the question is no longer merely whether you are sorry about yesterday.
It is whether you are willing to surrender tomorrow.
The sin you keep planning may be the very chain you keep asking Jesus to break.
